title: Protein structure and function
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM08a#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM08a#t3 term and clue written for the game; BM08a#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM08a#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM08a#N.4b, BM08a#N.10b, BM08a#N.12b, BM08a#N.13.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Primary structure
items.clue: The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, held by peptide bonds

items.label: Tertiary structure
items.clue: Overall 3D shape of one folded chain, held by bonds between R groups

items.label: α-helix
items.clue: Coil of the chain in which backbone hydrogen bonds hold each turn to the next

items.label: Denaturation
items.clue: Loss of a protein's shape at high temperature or changed pH; peptide bonds stay intact

questions.stem: Alpha-helices are found in many proteins whose amino acid sequences are very different from one another. Which statement best explains why alpha-helices can form in polypeptides with such different sequences?

options.text: A helix is held by bonds between R groups, and every kind of R group can form those bonds equally well.
A helix forms wherever the folding chain happens to coil at random, whatever the sequence.
A helix is formed by the peptide bonds, which join neighboring amino acids together in every chain.
A helix is held by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms, which are present whatever the R groups are.

questions.stem: A strong acid is added to a solution of an enzyme that normally works at about pH 7, lowering the pH to 1. The enzyme loses all of its activity. Which statement best describes what has happened to the enzyme?

options.text: Its peptide bonds are broken, so it has been split up into its separate amino acids.
It has been killed by the acid, in the same way that a strong acid kills living cells.
It is inhibited but not denatured, as only high temperature can denature enzymes.
Its folded shape is disrupted, although its amino acids are still joined in sequence.

questions.stem: A hypothetical enzyme has its highest rate of reaction at 40 °C. At 45 °C, its rate is lower. Which statement best explains the lower rate at 45 °C?

options.text: Enzyme and substrate molecules move so fast that they pass each other before they are able to bind.
Some hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's shape are disrupted, so the active site fits less well.
Some peptide bonds between the enzyme's amino acids break, splitting its chain into pieces.
Some of the enzyme molecules have been killed by the heat, so fewer are left alive to react.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces one amino acid in an enzyme at a position on the surface far from the active site in the folded protein. The enzyme loses most of its activity. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The result must be an error, because only the amino acids of the active site itself can affect catalysis
The change disturbs interactions that hold the enzyme's overall shape, altering the active site
The loss of activity shows the enzyme has been denatured, so its chain has broken up into free amino acids
The changed amino acid supplies less energy to the reaction, so the substrate cannot react
